_comment: Storage Windows fills by itself (AGENTS.md: patterns are data). The Windows twin of the Mac's system-storage.json, shown as 'What Windows keeps' in the Where's the rest? sheet. Research and sources: docs/STORAGE-RESEARCH-PLAN.md section 2. Paths take %SystemDrive%, %SystemRoot%, %LOCALAPPDATA% and the other variables UserFolders.Expand knows; a trailing * in the last component matches by prefix. action: never = Windows manages it, nothing to do; guide = free it through Windows' own settings (steps); trash = may be added to the basket (the Recycle Bin), and only when the path is outside CleanupQueue's excluded list. settingsUri: an ms-settings: page, opened by the shell (anything else is dropped when the file loads). measure: false = never sized (WinSxS: hard links make any folder walk over-count; only DISM /AnalyzeComponentStore, run as administrator, measures it, and the app never runs it). The Delivery Optimization cache path is from third-party sources (plan section 10): if it's wrong it's simply not found.

entries.title: Previous Windows installation
entries.why: The Windows you had before the last upgrade, kept so you can go back to it. Windows removes it by itself about 10 days after the upgrade.
steps: Open Settings › System › Storage › Temporary files.
Tick Previous Windows installation(s) and choose Remove files. You can't go back to the earlier version afterwards.

entries.title: Windows upgrade files
entries.why: Files Windows Setup downloads and unpacks to upgrade Windows. Windows protects them, so freedisk.space leaves them to Windows' own cleanup.
steps: Open Settings › System › Storage › Temporary files.
Tick Temporary Windows installation files and choose Remove files.

entries.title: Windows Update downloads
entries.why: Updates Windows has downloaded, and Delivery Optimization's cache of update files it can share with other PCs. Windows clears the cache by itself and caps it at a share of the disk.
steps: Open Settings › System › Storage › Temporary files.
Tick Windows Update Cleanup and Delivery Optimization Files and choose Remove files.

entries.title: Recall snapshots
entries.why: The snapshots Recall saves of your screen, encrypted on this PC. Removing its files by hand breaks Recall instead of freeing space cleanly, so they never go to the basket.
steps: Open Settings › Privacy & security › Recall & snapshots.
Delete snapshots there, or lower how much storage Recall may use.

entries.title: Component store (WinSxS)
entries.why: The files Windows needs to install updates and turn features on or off. Explorer shows it much bigger than it is: most files here are hard links to the same data in Windows' own folders, so they're counted twice. Only DISM /AnalyzeComponentStore, run as administrator, measures it.
steps: Never delete files here: Windows can stop updating or starting.
Windows cleans it up on a schedule. To do it now, open Disk Cleanup, choose Clean up system files and tick Windows Update Cleanup.

entries.title: Windows Installer cache
entries.why: Copies of the installers (.msi and .msp) of your programs and their updates. Windows Installer needs them to repair, update or uninstall those programs.
steps: Nothing to do: uninstalling a program you no longer use removes its copies too.

entries.title: Windows logs
entries.why: Logs Windows writes while it installs updates, features and drivers (CBS, DISM and others). They're how a failed update gets diagnosed.
steps: Nothing to do: leave them to Windows.
